content: 1. Complications of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE): An updated study from the Hopkins Lupus Cohort highlights the complications associated with SLE, including arthritis and vascular diseases. (Arthritis Care Res. 1995;8:137–45). 2. Contraception in SLE Patients: Research by Mintz et al. (1984) explored the use of progestogen-based contraception in women with SLE, emphasizing its safety and efficacy. (Contraception. 1984;30:29–38). 3. Peripheral Vascular Disease in SLE: McDonald et al. (1992) identified peripheral vascular disease as a significant complication in SLE patients. (Ann Rheum Dis. 1992;51:56–60). 4. Environmental Factors and Lupus Nephritis: McAlindon et al. investigated environmental predictors of nephritis in SLE patients, emphasizing the role of external factors in disease progression. (Ann Rheum Dis). 5. Cardiovascular Risks in SLE: Manzi et al. (1997) compared age-specific rates of myocardial infarction and angina in women with SLE to the Framingham Study, revealing increased cardiovascular risks. (Am J Epidemiol. 1997;145:408–15). 6. Oral Contraceptives and SLE Activity: Jungers et al. (1982) studied the influence of oral contraceptives on SLE activity, finding no significant exacerbation of the disease. (Arthritis Rheum. 1982;25:618–23). 7. Contraceptive Practices in SLE: Julkunen et al. (1993) examined contraceptive use among women with SLE, highlighting the importance of tailored contraceptive options. (Br J Rheumatol. 1993;32:227–30). 8. Hormonal Contraceptives and SLE: Julkunen (1991) reviewed the side effects and impact of oral contraceptives on SLE activity, emphasizing the need for careful monitoring. (Scand J Rheumatol. 1991;20:427–33). 9. Atherosclerosis in SLE: Esdaile et al. (2001) demonstrated that traditional Framingham risk factors do not fully explain accelerated atherosclerosis in SLE patients. (Arthritis Rheum. 2001;44:2331–7). 10. Thrombosis Risk in Antiphospholipid Syndrome: Chopra et al. (2002) explored the role of Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations in thrombosis risk among patients with antiphospholipid antibodies. (J Rheumatol. 2002;29:1683–8). 11. Abnormal Pap Results in SLE: Bernatsky et al. (2004) identified factors associated with abnormal Pap smear results in women with SLE, emphasizing the need for regular screening. (Rheumatology (Oxford). 2004;43:1386–9). 12. Bernatsky et al. (Rheumatology (Oxford). 2004;43:1178–81). 13. Venous Thrombosis and Antiphospholipid Antibodies: Wahl et al. (1997) conducted a meta-analysis on the risk of venous thrombosis in SLE patients with antiphospholipid antibodies. (Lupus. 1997;6:467–73). 14. Lupus Nephritis and Raynaud’s Phenomenon: Choojitarn et al. (2008) identified lupus nephritis and Raynaud’s phenomenon as significant risk factors for vascular thrombosis in SLE patients with antiphospholipid antibodies. (Clin Rheumatol. 2008;27(3):345–51). 15. Levonorgestrel-Releasing Intrauterine System (LNG-IUS) for Menorrhagia: Studies have compared the LNG-IUS with other treatments like thermal balloon ablation and endometrial resection, demonstrating its effectiveness in managing menorrhagia. (Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol. 2003;108(1):72–4; Int J Gynaecol Obstet. 2006;95(3):261–6). 16. Quality of Life and Cost-Effectiveness of LNG-IUS: Hurskainen et al. (2001) found that LNG-IUS improves quality of life and is cost-effective compared to hysterectomy for menorrhagia treatment. (Lancet. 2001;357(9252):273–7). 17. LNG-IUS in Endometriosis: Research has shown the efficacy of LNG-IUS in treating symptoms of endometriosis, including dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. (Fertil Steril. 2001;75(3):485–8; Hum Reprod. 2005;20(7):1993–8). 18. Copper IUD for Emergency Contraception: Copper-bearing IUDs are highly effective for emergency contraception when inserted within five days of unprotected intercourse. However, they do not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. (Contraception). 19. Progesterone-Releasing Vaginal Ring (PVR): The PVR is a contraceptive option for breastfeeding women, releasing 10 mg/day of progesterone and inhibiting ovulation. It is worn continuously for three months and does not affect breastfeeding performance or infant growth. (Contraception). 20. Barrier Methods and STI Protection: Correct and consistent use of condoms is recommended for STI prevention, including HIV. Female condoms are effective but less widely used than male condoms. (Contraception). 21. HIV and Contraceptive Use: Studies have explored the relationship between contraceptive methods and HIV transmission, shedding light on the safety and appropriateness of options like IUDs and hormonal contraceptives for HIV-infected women. (Lancet; Am J Obstet Gynecol). 22. WHO Guidelines on Contraceptive Use: The World Health Organization has developed medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, emphasizing evidence-based recommendations for various populations, including breastfeeding women and those with specific medical conditions. (WHO). This summary provides a detailed and professional interpretation of the provided references, focusing on the key findings and implications for clinical practice.
